# Stage: inbox

**Purpose.** Decide whether each arrival becomes work. An arrival is not work
yet, so this stage takes no work item reference.

**Inputs.** Every arrival waiting in the inbox, and whatever in the repository
helps you understand one well enough to decide.
Each arrival is an item at the inbox stage: `tcw work list --stage inbox`
lists them, and `tcw work path <slug> request` names the request each carries.

**Produce** no document. The outcome is each arrival accepted, turned away, or
left for a person, and a short report saying which and why.

## Steps

1. Read every arrival. One that describes several unrelated changes is several
   pieces of work; one change with several parts is one.
2. Check the board before accepting anything: `tcw work list`, then
   `tcw work show <slug>` for a likely match. An arrival already tracked is
   recorded on the existing item, with `tcw work comment <slug>` (the text on
   stdin), not accepted a second time.
3. Choose every tag that applies from `tcw work tags list`. Register a new
   one only if it will earn its place beyond this arrival.
4. Accept.
   `tcw work advance <slug>` moves the item to request. Add tags with
   `tcw work edit <slug> --tag <tag>`. For each extra piece of a split
   arrival, `tcw work new "<title>"` with its part of the text on stdin.
5. Turn away a duplicate, or something the project will not do.
   `tcw work discard <slug> --reason "<why>"`, naming the existing item for a
   duplicate.
6. Do not ask whoever filed it for more detail. They are usually not present
   to answer; the request stage asks.

## Exit badly

- _Too vague to decide._ Do not invent scope.
  Accept it and leave the questions for request, or leave it where it is and
  say why.
- _You cannot tell whether it is already tracked._ Leave it, and name the
  items you suspect it overlaps.

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: request

**Purpose.** Record what is being asked for and why, at a product level and for
any reader, before anyone decides what to build. Keep code references light
unless the work is technical by nature.

**Inputs.** What the item asks for, as `tcw work show <slug>` prints it, and the
person asking. Repository discovery is unrestricted.

**Resuming.** Read the newest handoff first, as a description of the work when
it was written, and check for anything newer before trusting it.
It is the newest `handoff-*.md` beside the file `tcw work path <slug> request`
names. To leave one, write it to `tcw work path <slug> request --handoff`.

**Produce** the request, in five sections:

- **What and why**: the change, and the reason for it.
- **Product changes**: what users will be able to do differently, and what the
  change adds, changes or removes. "None" is a valid answer; write it as such.
- **Out of scope**: what is deliberately left out.
- **Constraints**: deadlines, compatibility, anything that limits the answer.
- **References**: each with one line on why it matters.
Write it to `tcw work path <slug> request`. Keep any dated `## Added`
sections already there: they are amendments made after it was written.

## Steps

1. **Ask the user what is unclear.** This stage exists to get input only they
   have.
2. **Ask for reference material**: docs, an issue, prior work, a related item.
   Do not fetch or judge it here. If there is none, write "asked; none
   provided" under References, so spec can tell that from never asking.
3. Write in the requester's terms. Do not specify a solution; that is spec's
   job, and doing it here hides the alternatives.

## Exit badly

- _The request contradicts something already true of the product._ Say so and
  ask, rather than recording a request nobody can satisfy.
- _The work is larger than one item._ Say so now; splitting after a spec is
  written wastes the spec.
- _There is no user to ask._ Write from the evidence available and mark each
  assumption, so spec knows which parts are inference.

> **When this stage's output is written, run `tcw work advance <slug>`.**

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: spec

**Purpose.** Decide _what_ to build and why, technically, before deciding how.
A spec that describes an implementation has skipped its own job.

**Inputs.** The request, read as filed:

`tcw work show <slug>` prints it.

Its References are where research starts, not where it ends; with neither
references nor an "asked; none provided" note, nobody asked. Repository
discovery is unrestricted.

**Resuming.** Read the newest `handoff-*.md` beside the file
`tcw work path <slug> spec` names, as a description of the work when it was
written, and check for anything newer before trusting it. To leave one, write
it to `tcw work path <slug> spec --handoff`.

**Produce** three things:

- The spec, at `tcw work path <slug> spec`, with seven sections: **Capability
  changes**, **Problem**, **Goals**, **Non-goals**, **Design**, **Acceptance
  criteria**, **Risks**.
- `capabilities.yaml`, in the folder `tcw work path <slug>` prints: the
  capability paths this work adds, changes or removes, under `new:`,
  `changed:` and `removed:`, and taxonomy terms under `taxonomy:` the same
  way. It declares; it writes no records. Implement changes the records.
- **The QA plan**, posted with `tcw work comment <slug>` (the text on stdin),
  for readers outside engineering. Its first line is `QA plan`. It gives one
  scenario per product change in the request, the expected behavior of each,
  the environment or accounts needed, and what is not tested. With no product
  changes, it says so and names what qa should confirm did not change. A
  revised spec posts a new QA plan whose second line names the one it replaces.

## Steps

1. **Product first.** For each product change, check the project's taxonomy
   and capabilities for the terms and capabilities it touches.
2. Read the request's references, then the code the change touches. **Ground
   every claim about current behavior in the code, with file and line.**
3. Write acceptance criteria someone else can check without asking what you
   meant. "Works correctly" is not one.
4. State what is out of scope, especially anything close enough to drift in.
5. **A sweep for defects like the reported one is repository-wide by default**,
   or the spec says why it was narrowed.
6. **Self-review.** Every file and line cited still shows what you claim;
   every criterion you can run against the code today has been run; any
   criterion two readers could check two ways is pinned to one.

## Exit badly

- _The code contradicts the request._ Stop and return to request. A spec that
  quietly reinterprets the request is worse than one that refuses.
- _The requester revises the request._ It stays at spec: record it as an
  amendment (a dated `## Added`; in Jira, an `Added` comment), and follow it.
- _The work is too large for one item._ Say so; plan decomposes it.
- _You cannot ground a claim._ Mark it as an assumption, not a fact.
- _`tcw work comment` failed._ Report the command and its exit code, do not
  advance, and leave the spec as written. Running this stage again posts the
  QA plan.

> **When this stage's output is written, run `tcw work advance <slug>`.**

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: plan

**Purpose.** Decide _how_, in ordered steps someone else could follow, so that
sequencing problems are found here and not halfway through implementing.

**Inputs.** The spec, at `tcw work path <slug> spec`, and the request:

`tcw work show <slug>` prints it.

Repository discovery is unrestricted.

**Resuming.** Read the newest `handoff-*.md` beside the file
`tcw work path <slug> plan` names, as a description of the work when it was
written, and check for anything newer before trusting it. To leave one, write
it to `tcw work path <slug> plan --handoff`.

**Produce** the plan, at `tcw work path <slug> plan`: ordered steps, each naming
the **exact files it creates or changes** and what proves it is done; a
**Documentation Sync** block; and a **Verification** section for anything the
tests cannot check.

## Steps

1. Order the steps so the tests pass after each one. A step that leaves things
   broken for the next is two steps.
2. Put the riskiest change where it is _isolated_: after what it depends on
   exists and its tests are written.
3. Evaluate every Documentation Sync entry in the project's agent guide
   (`AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`) and name a step for each trigger that will
   fire. Where the TCW plugin is installed, invoke the `documentation-sync` skill
   to do this. Schedule those steps as one block at the end.
4. If `capabilities.yaml` is missing from the folder `tcw work path <slug>`
   prints and the request names product changes, write it now, as spec would.
   If the item has no `QA plan` comment in `tcw work show <slug>`, post one
   with `tcw work comment <slug>`, as spec would.
5. Record dependencies between items as blockers, not prose:
   `tcw work edit <slug> --blocked-by <ref>`.
6. **Too large for one item?** Split it here: `tcw work new "<title>" --parent
   <slug> --nest` per part, request on stdin. `--nest`, passed every time, puts
   the part's folder inside the parent's folder (or says why not); `--parent`,
   not the folder, is what makes it a part. A part for another project is made
   in that project:
   `tcw -C tcw://<id>.path/ work new "<title>" --parent <slug> --nest`
   (`--nest` then makes it at the top of that project's store and says so);
   set `--blocked-by` the same way. When Jira cannot link the parent (an epic
   kept in files, or on another Jira site), TCW records it in the part's
   folder and says so, and Jira itself does not show it.
7. **No placeholders.** "TBD", "add error handling", "as in step 3": a step
   nobody can carry out without asking you a question is not a step.
8. **Self-review.** Re-read the plan against the spec: every acceptance
   criterion is covered by a step and every step traces back to one; names
   are consistent; no step appears twice.

## Exit badly

- _Planning shows the spec is wrong._ Return to spec and fix it:
  `tcw work advance <slug> --to spec`. Do not plan around a spec you have
  stopped believing.
- _A step cannot be verified._ Say so in the step rather than inventing a test
  that would pass either way.

> **When this stage's output is written, run `tcw work advance <slug>`.**

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: implement

**Purpose.** Build it, and record what happened, including where the plan
was wrong.

**Inputs.** The spec and plan (`tcw work path <slug> spec` and `plan`), the
earlier rounds in `tcw work path <slug> implement`, and the latest rejection,
which is what makes a later round different from the first. Repository
discovery is unrestricted. **The latest rejection** is every review or qa round
saying `verdict: rejected` whose `judges` is the newest implement round's number
(in `tcw work path <slug> review` and `qa`).

**Resuming.** Read the newest `handoff-*.md` in `tcw work path <slug> implement`
as a description of the work when it was written; check for anything newer
before trusting it. Leave one at `tcw work path <slug> implement --handoff`.

**Produce** the code, the record changes, and one round at
`tcw work path <slug> implement --next`, with no verdict. The round says what
was done, step by step; the test result, from a command run just now; what the
plan or spec got wrong; which records changed; and which rejections it answers,
each by its round file or, for a comment, by its time as `tcw work show` prints
it. **Write the round once, at the end**, when the work it describes is
finished: never first, to fill in later.

## Steps

1. Work the plan's steps in order.
2. **Change the taxonomy and capability records in the same change as the
   code**, as `capabilities.yaml` in the folder `tcw work path <slug>` prints
   declares, so review finds them true. Write that file first if no earlier
   stage did. Give every new capability its status, normally `Supported`.
3. **Write the failing test first and watch it fail** before the code that
   makes it pass. A test that has never been red proves nothing. When a new
   test passes on its first run, break the behaviour it names and confirm it
   goes red before writing anything else.
4. On a bug or unexpected failure, **find the root cause before the fix**, and
   fix it where every caller goes through, not where it was reported.
5. **When the code disproves the plan, fix the plan and say so.** Working
   around it silently is how documents start lying.
6. Check each capability change against the standing records for
   contradictions.
7. **Once every step is done and the tests pass,**
   evaluate every Documentation Sync entry in the project's agent guide
   (`AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`) once, against the whole finished change. Where the TCW plugin is
   installed, invoke the `documentation-sync` skill to do this.
8. **No claim that something works without output from a command run just now.**
9. Write the round. **Self-review:** an empty "what the plan or spec got wrong"
   is a claim, not an omission.

## Exit badly

- _The plan is unworkable._ Return to plan with
  `tcw work advance <slug> --to plan`; do not build a different design and
  leave the plan describing the abandoned one.
- _A step is blocked by other work._ Record it
  (`tcw work edit <slug> --blocked-by <ref>`), finish the rest, and say what
  was left out.
- _Scope grew._ Build what was specified; create a follow-up item for the rest.

> **When this stage's output is written, run `tcw work advance <slug>`.**

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: review

**Purpose.** Check the code against the spec and the plan, including that the
taxonomy and capability records changed with it and say what the code does.
A move past implement already checked that the declared records exist; this
stage checks that they are right.

**Inputs.** The spec and plan (`tcw work path <slug> spec` and `plan`), the
newest round in `tcw work path <slug> implement`, `capabilities.yaml` in the
folder `tcw work path <slug>` prints, and the code itself. Read the change
through what the implement round says changed; how the project shows a change
to its reviewers is its own choice. Repository discovery is unrestricted.

**Resuming.** Read the newest `handoff-*.md` in `tcw work path <slug> review`,
as a description of the work when it was written, and check for anything newer
before trusting it. To leave one, write it to
`tcw work path <slug> review --handoff`.

**Produce** one round at `tcw work path <slug> review --next`, starting with
this front matter:

```yaml
---
verdict: accepted        # or rejected
judges: 3                # the newest implement round
---
```

`judges` is the highest `N` among the `round-N.md` files in
`tcw work path <slug> implement`, or 0 when there are none. A wrong number
makes the verdict stale, and a stale verdict lets nothing through. Under the
front matter, list each acceptance criterion as met, not met, or not
checkable, with the evidence for each.

**Who reviews.** A reviewer that did not write the code: a separate agent
where you can start one, given this stage's instructions and able only to read.
Where you cannot, read the change afresh against the spec in this session, and
say plainly in the round that the author reviewed it.

## Steps

1. Run the project's checks. **No claim without output from a command you ran
   just now.**
2. Go through the acceptance criteria one at a time, against the code, not
   against the implement round's account of it.
3. Check every path in `capabilities.yaml` against its record: present, and
   describing what the code now does. A record that names behavior the code
   does not have is a rejection.
4. Decide. `accepted` only when every criterion is met or the round says why
   one that is not checkable does not matter. Otherwise `rejected`, saying
   what implement must do.
5. Write the round. You may record the verdict yourself.

## Exit badly

- _A criterion cannot be checked as written._ Say so in the round; it is a spec
  defect worth recording, not something to wave through.
- _The spec solved the wrong problem._ A rejection will not fix that. Say so,
  and return the item to spec with `tcw work advance <slug> --to spec`.

> **When this stage's output is written, run `tcw work advance <slug>`.** The verdict decides where the item goes, so write the round first.

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: qa

**Purpose.** Check the product's behavior against the request and the QA plan:
what a user will now be able to do, tried the way a user would.

**Inputs.** The request's Product changes, from `tcw work show <slug>`, and the
newest comment there whose first line is `QA plan`. With no QA plan, test
against the request's Product changes and say so.

**Resuming.** Read the newest handoff first, as a description of the work when
it was written, and check for anything newer before trusting it.
It is the newest `handoff-*.md` in `tcw work path <slug> qa`. To leave one,
write it to `tcw work path <slug> qa --handoff`.

**Produce** one round at `tcw work path <slug> qa --next`, starting with the
front matter review uses:

```yaml
---
verdict: accepted        # or rejected
judges: 3                # the newest implement round
---
```

`judges` is the highest `N` among the `round-N.md` files in
`tcw work path <slug> implement`, or 0 when there are none. Under it, list each
QA plan scenario as passed, failed or not run, with the evidence for each.

## Steps

1. Run each scenario in the QA plan, in the environment it names.
2. Judge the product against the request's Product changes and each
   scenario's expected behavior. **No claim without output or an observation
   from just now.**
3. `accepted` only when every scenario passed, or the round says why one not
   run does not matter. Otherwise `rejected`, saying what implement must fix.
4. Write the round. By default you record the verdict yourself. If the
   project's instructions for this stage say a person decides the verdict:
   run the scenarios, present the evidence, ask the person for `accepted` or
   `rejected` with a reason, and write the round at `qa --next` recording
   their decision, with `decided-by: <their name>` beside `verdict` and
   `judges`. Do not choose the verdict for them. If they do not answer, write
   no round and say so.

## Exit badly

- _A scenario cannot be run_ (no environment, no account). Record it as not
  run and say what is missing; do not mark it passed.
- _The product does what the spec says but not what the request asked._ That
  is a finding for the person deciding, and for a postmortem.

> **When this stage's output is written, run `tcw work advance <slug>`.** The verdict decides where the item goes, so write the round first.

> **This text ran no checks.** Gates run when an item moves; `tcw work advance <slug> --dry-run` reports whether the next move would pass, and what would stop it.

# Stage: postmortem

**Purpose.** Find which stage first missed a problem. Not blame and not a
summary: the question is _where would this have been cheapest to catch_. This
stage never moves the item, nothing waits on it, and it applies to any item
that was not discarded, finished or not.

**Inputs.** The item, read **backwards**: qa rounds, then review rounds, then
implement rounds (`tcw work path <slug> <stage>` for each); then the plan, the
spec and the request; then the item's comments, from `tcw work show <slug>`.
**`## Notes` across them is the primary trail**: where each stage recorded what
it knew at the time, often a detail noticed and not pursued. Also read:

- what an implement round says the plan or spec got wrong: was it knowably
  wrong when it was written?
- the spec's acceptance criteria: if work that met every one was rejected, the
  criteria were the defect;
- a missing document: a spec absent from an item that needed one is itself the
  finding.

**Resuming.** Read the newest `handoff-*.md` beside the file
`tcw work path <slug> postmortem` names, as a description of the work when it
was written, and check for anything newer before trusting it. To leave one,
write it to `tcw work path <slug> postmortem --handoff`.

**Produce** the postmortem, at `tcw work path <slug> postmortem`: what went
wrong; which stage could first have caught it; what would have had to be
different; and whether that change is worth making.

## Steps

1. Find the earliest stage whose documents could have shown the problem.
2. **Tell "nobody could have known" from "nobody checked."** Ask of that
   stage: was the information there at that point? If the code that disproved
   a spec claim existed and was readable, the spec could have checked:
   actionable. If the failure showed only once it was built, no earlier stage
   could have caught it, and the honest finding is that the process worked.
3. Write the postmortem. Create follow-up items with `tcw work new` for
   anything worth changing.
4. **What the request missed.** Only when the project's instructions for this
   stage ask for it: post a comment with `tcw work comment <slug>` saying what
   the request missed, written in the request's own language for its readers.

## Exit badly

Stop without a recommendation, and say why, when:

- the cause is a one-off; record it and stop;
- the only recommendation left is "be more careful", which is a wish, not a
  change: the cause has not been found yet;
- the fix costs more than the failures it would prevent; that is a real
  conclusion, not a failure to reach one.

> **Nothing follows this stage.** It never moves the item; write its document and stop.
